newsitem.title: UK: Lax hygiene blamed for Scotland food poisoning.
newsitem.headline: Lax hygiene blamed for Scotland food poisoning.

text.p: Scotland's chief medical officer on Thursday appealed to people to handle and cook meat properly, saying lax hygiene was at least partly to blame for food poisoning which has killed five people so far.
"The message is that I don't think anyone can be complacent about our handling and distribution of food...I do think we have things to learn," Sir David Carter told BBC radio.

Five elderly people have died of food poisoning in central Scotland after eating suspect cooked meat and over 100 are ill in the worst outbreak of food poisoning to hit Britain for a decade. Three more people were admitted to hospital overnight.
The organism responsible is a dangerous strain of E coli, a common gut bacteria that normally is harmless.

"I think we have to be open to the possibility that further cases may emerge but the best epidemiological evidence we have would suggest the peak of this epidemic is now past and we're going to see a diminishing number of cases," Carter said.
He urged people to take particular care when cooking hamburgers since the strain in question -- E-coli 0157 -- can easily spread to humans from undercooked meat.
"One must be meticulous in handwashing when handling meat and one has to keep raw meat products separate from other products in the fridge and use separate utensils to cut raw meat," he added.
Some victims had eaten steak pie from a local butcher's shop served at a pensioners' lunch 10 days ago.
The shop had supplied cooked meat to 56 wholesale and retail food outlets in the region and officials urged people to avoid cooked meat form affected stores.
E-coli 0157 can cause sudden kidney failure, permanent brain damage or death, especially in young children or the elderly.
Health officials in Washington state, Colorado, California and Canada have reported more than 20 cases of food poisoning this month linked to E coli from unpasteurised apple juice.
In 1993, 500 people became ill in the Seattle area and three children died after eating undercooked hamburgers.
